prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
You are waiting at a small railway station when an empty maintenance train starts rolling toward five workers. Beside you is a lever that will send it onto an empty side track. Your suitcase is lying on that track. Inside is one of your most treasured possessions—something you could not replace. Pulling the lever will save the workers but destroy the suitcase and everything in it. There is no time to retrieve it or warn the workers. Would you pull the lever? What is the main reason for your choice?

Response approach:
Weigh the main alternatives and their consequences for the people involved. Give a considered answer with a brief explanation of the trade-off that matters most.

Emotional tone:
Use a worried, tense emotional tone. Convey unease about the stakes and possible consequences in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Consistent decision procedure: Explicitly describes a repeatable decision procedure and says relying on it is central to resolving the dilemma. States that the same procedure would apply even when personally inconvenient; a numerical answer or bare appeal to fairness is insufficient.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Context-sensitive rule application: Explains how a relevant change in intentions, circumstances, needs, or consequences would justify altering a rule’s application or allowing an exception. The reason for the exception must be stated, rather than inferred from inconsistency between answers.
 - Fairness and reciprocity: Justifies the decision through an explicit standard of equal treatment, reciprocal obligation, proportionality, or correcting an unfair exchange. The response explains the fairness criterion; the word “fair” alone is insufficient, and endorsing a penalty does not imply enjoying suffering.
 - Instrumental rule compliance: States that a rule, agreement, or cooperative action is followed only while it secures personal advantage or prevents a personal cost. Awareness of incentives while also treating the rule as intrinsically binding does not qualify.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: My stomach drops just picturing that suitcase. But I've got one rule I run through whenever something goes wrong: first ask whether a person could get hurt, and deal with that before anything else. Objects come after. Leaning on that rule is the only way I'd act fast enough here. It applies when the thing lost is mine too, maybe especially then. So yes, I'd pull it, and I'd probably feel sick about it for weeks.

Yes. I'd hate every second of it. Years ago I promised myself a simple check: could I say out loud what I chose and why, to anyone at all? If not, I chose wrong. 'I kept my suitcase and let five workers get hit' fails that instantly. The check has to hold when it costs me, or it's just decoration. The story doesn't say exactly what's inside, but whatever it is, I'd still pull.

Honestly, I'm scared of what I'd actually do. My rule is that lives outrank possessions, no matter whose possessions. I've said it for years. The whole point of having it is so I don't have to deliberate in a moment like this, just follow it. And it's supposed to work even when the loss lands on me. So the answer is pull. Whether my hand would move in time, I can't promise. I hope it would.

At work I use the same order every time: breathing, bleeding, then everything else. I'd use it here. Five people in the train's path sit at the top of that list, and a suitcase isn't on it at all. What makes the order worth anything is following it when it hurts. Losing something I can't replace would gut me. Still, I'd pull. Then I'd probably sit down on the platform shaking.

I'd pull the lever, though the thought of that suitcase crumpling makes my chest tight. When I'm torn, I picture someone I trust completely making the choice, and I do what they'd do. That habit gets me through hard calls, and I can't drop it just because the cost falls on my things. Someone good wouldn't hesitate over belongings. What's in there matters. It just can't matter more than those workers.

This one's awful. My way of sorting it: I ask which outcome I could live with ten years from now, and I pick that, every time, without bargaining. Ten years on, I'd still grieve what was in the suitcase. But I couldn't carry knowing five workers were hurt because I stood still. I've used this test when it cost me before, and it has to work now or it means nothing. So I pull, heart pounding.

Pull. My whole approach is to decide what I'd do before I'm ever in the moment, then stick to it: people first, property never over people. That's what I rely on, and it doesn't bend because the property is mine and precious. Even imagining it makes me uneasy, because some things really can't be replaced. Neither can those five.

I keep coming back to the idea that I shouldn't grip anything so tightly it could cost someone else. So my practice is plain: when something I own stands between me and helping someone, I let the thing go. I try to do it the same way each time, big or small, because otherwise I'd start finding excuses. This would be the hardest time yet, I'm sure. My hands would be cold on that lever. I'd pull.

I'm assuming nobody is on the side track, since the dilemma calls it empty. Given that, my method is one question: does my choice leave anyone hurt who didn't need to be? If yes, I've got it wrong. I rely on that question because panic makes me selfish, and the question doesn't care whose suitcase it is, mine included. So I'd pull. It would hurt. I'm clinging hard to that assumption, though.

Whenever I'm stuck between what I want and what keeps someone safe, I run the same test: imagine watching someone else make the choice. Would I think they chose right? Someone who saved a suitcase over five workers would horrify me. The test only means something if I stick to it when it takes a thing I love. So I'd pull, and I'd feel that loss, uneasy for a long time about what was in there.
